name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
title: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
answer: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool as a question asking coach rather than an interpreter, so students still do the reading, reasoning, and writing themselves. It matters because primary sources are the raw material of history and reading them well is a skill built over years, and because AI can otherwise do the interpreting for students instead of helping them learn to do it.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Primary sources such as letters, speeches, photographs, and government records are the raw material of history, and reading them well is a skill students build over years. Large collections of these sources are available free of charge from the Library of Congress and many state archives. The idea is to use AI to help students work with these sources without letting it do the interpreting for them. A school configured tool acts as a coach, asking the kinds of questions a historian would ask, such as who created a document and when, what the author was trying to accomplish, what it leaves out, and who might see it differently. The student answers and the coach asks follow up questions, but the tool never tells the student what the source means.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, document based questions work well with this approach. A teacher can set up a hint only tool, as described in Chapter 7, that helps students plan an essay using a set of documents without writing the essay itself. The tool might ask which documents support the student's argument and which complicate it, while the student does the reading, the reasoning, and the writing. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea. Teachers choose the sources themselves, and every source students use should come from an archive, a library database, or a trusted collection.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, or figure for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing how a school configured coach and a hint only tool can be used with primary sources and document based questions.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Teachers should choose the sources themselves rather than letting the tool supply them. AI tools can suggest documents, but they sometimes describe documents that do not exist or misquote real ones, so every source students use should come from an archive, a library database, or a trusted collection. The coach helps students read real sources, not invented ones. The interpreting stays with the student, and the tool does not tell the student what the source means. The decisions about which sources to use and how to frame the work stay with the teacher.
